To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
photosynthesis versus irradiance (P‐I) curves measured by O2 production, pulse‐amplitude modulated (PAM), and 14C methods show similar relative temperature responses for three microalgal species.

the temperature response of the maximum photosynthetic capacity is similar for three different approaches (O2 production, PAM, and 14 C incorporation), and that a lower quantum yield of O2 production in comparison to 14C assimilated carbon can explain the offset of absolute rates measured by O2 production and PAM‐based calculations.

the maximum photosynthetic rates of three marine phytoplankter species were strongly stimulated by temperature and showed a similar response to temperature when measured by O2 production, pulse‐amplitude modulated fluorescence, and 14‐C incorporation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the temperature effects on photosynthetic light responses of three marine microalgae.
the effects of short‐term temperature variations on photosynthetic parameters in three microalgae.
the effects of temperature on the photosynthesis–irradiance relationship of microalgae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the PAM‐based approach provides an excellent alternative to the conventional methods of O2‐production and 14C measurements for studying photosynthetic responses of microalgae to light and temperature.

the three applied methods (O2‐production measurements, 14C‐assimilation measurements, and PAM‐fluorometry measurements) can provide similar information on temperature effects on photosynthetic light responses in microalgae.
all three methods are suitable for measuring short‐term photosynthesis in microalgal monocultures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PAM‐based method is a valuable tool to study photosynthesis in microalgal monocultures, and it is a promising method to study photosynthetic processes in microalgal communities.
the three methods used in this study are all applicable for measuring temperature effects on microalgal photosynthesis.
the PAM technique provides a good alternative to measure photosynthetic light responses in microalgae.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the temperature response of PCmax is similar for the three applied techniques, whereas αC is less temperature‐sensitive and shows a species‐specific response.
the temperature sensitivity of photosynthetic parameters is species dependent, with Pro. minimum being the only species showing a temperature‐dependent optimum.

the PAM technique is an excellent tool for the study of short‐term temperature effects, but the results should be interpreted with respect to the species‐specific offset between O2 production and PAM‐based photosynthesis.
